section.title: The Resurrection of the Dead
section.sectionRationale: Having laid down the resurrection of Christ as bedrock, Paul now confronts those in Corinth who deny a resurrection of the dead. He shows that the two stand or fall together: if the dead are not raised, then Christ is not raised, and the whole faith collapses into futility. But Christ has been raised, the firstfruits, and His resurrection guarantees the harvest. As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive, until He has put every enemy, last of all death, under His feet, and God is all in all.
section.thesis: The resurrection of Christ and the resurrection of His people cannot be separated: deny one and you lose both, and with them all hope; but Christ has truly been raised as the firstfruits, so that as in Adam all die, in Christ all will be made alive, and the risen Lord will reign until the last enemy, death, is destroyed and God is all in all.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the collapse if Christ is not raised; but Christ is raised, the firstfruits, undoing Adam's death; the reign of Christ until every enemy, last of all death, is subdued; and the call to holy living in light of the resurrection hope.

units.label: If Christ has not been raised

verses.text: But if it is preached that Christ has been {{egeiro|raised}} from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no {{anastasis|resurrection}} of the dead?
If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.
And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith.
In that case, we are also exposed as false witnesses about God. For we have testified about God that He raised Christ from the dead, but He did not raise Him if in fact the dead are not raised.
For if the dead are not raised, then not even Christ has been raised.
And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.
Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.
If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.

units.label: But Christ has been raised, the firstfruits
units.note: in Adam all die, in Christ all made alive

verses.text: But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the {{aparche|firstfruits}} of those who have fallen asleep.
For since {{thanatos|death}} came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man.
For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.
But each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him.

units.label: He must reign until death is destroyed
units.note: every enemy under His feet, God all in all

verses.text: Then the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power.
For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet.
The last enemy to be destroyed is {{thanatos|death}}.
For “God has put everything under His feet.” Now when it says that everything has been put under Him, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under Him.
And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.

units.label: Live in light of the resurrection
units.note: why risk everything, and stop sinning

verses.text: If these things are not so, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them?
And why do we endanger ourselves every hour?
I face death every day, brothers, as surely as I boast about you in Christ Jesus our Lord.
If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
Do not be deceived: “Bad company corrupts good character.”
Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God. I say this to your shame.

egeiro.gloss: To raise, to wake, to lift up. The drumbeat verb of the chapter. Paul rings the change on it again and again: Christ has been raised, and if the dead are not raised then not even Christ has been raised. The resurrection of Christ and of His people rise and fall together on this one word.

anastasis.gloss: A standing up, a rising, resurrection. The bodily raising of the dead to new life, not merely the survival of the soul. Some at Corinth denied there is any such thing; Paul insists that to deny the resurrection of the dead is to deny the resurrection of Christ, and so to empty the gospel.

aparche.gloss: Firstfruits, the first portion of the harvest offered to God as the pledge and guarantee of the full crop to come. To call the risen Christ the firstfruits is to say His resurrection is the first installment and sure promise of the resurrection of all who belong to Him; where the firstfruits have been raised, the harvest must follow.

thanatos.gloss: Death. In Paul death is not merely natural but an enemy, the last foe of God's people, the reign of the grave that entered through Adam's sin. The whole argument marches toward one triumphant claim: the last enemy to be destroyed is death, undone by the risen and reigning Christ.

basic.context: Some in Corinth were saying there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul shows they cannot hold that and still keep the gospel. If the dead are never raised, then Christ was never raised either, and if Christ was not raised, then the preaching is empty, faith is worthless, and believers are still lost in their sins. But Christ has been raised, and that changes everything. He is the firstfruits, the first of a great harvest. As death spread from Adam to all, so life spreads from Christ to all who are His.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul argues by drawing out consequences. He takes the Corinthian denial to its logical end to show how ruinous it is, then turns the corner with a triumphant but Christ has indeed been raised. He reasons from Adam to Christ, from firstfruits to harvest, and from the reign of Christ to the final destruction of death, ending with the practical point that if there is no resurrection, holiness and sacrifice make no sense.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter hammers the verb egeiro, to raise, again and again. The disputed word is anastasis, resurrection, the bodily rising some denied. Christ is the aparche, the firstfruits, the first sheaf that guarantees the whole harvest. And the great enemy is thanatos, death, which entered through Adam and will be the last foe destroyed by the reigning Christ.
basic.typology: Christ the firstfruits fulfills the Old Testament feast of firstfruits, when the first sheaf of harvest was offered as the pledge of the full crop. Adam and Christ stand as two heads of humanity: through the first, death; through the last, life. The reign of Christ until every enemy is under His feet fulfills the enthronement promised in Psalm 8 and Psalm 110.
basic.christ: Christ is the raised one on whom everything hangs. His resurrection is not an isolated wonder but the firstfruits, the beginning of the harvest of the dead. He is the new head of the human race, the last Adam, who undoes what the first Adam did. And He is the reigning Lord who must rule until every enemy, including death itself, is placed under His feet, before He hands the kingdom to the Father.
basic.god: It is God who raised Christ and who will raise us. God is putting everything under Christ's feet, and in the end the Son will hand the kingdom to the Father, so that God may be all in all. The goal of the whole drama is the unclouded reign of God over a redeemed creation, with death, the last enemy, forever destroyed.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 5 sets Adam and Christ side by side, death through one and life through the other. Psalm 110 and Psalm 8 promise a Lord who reigns until His enemies are His footstool. Revelation 20 and 21 show death itself thrown into the lake of fire and God dwelling with His people. Second Corinthians 4 speaks of the risen life that makes present suffering worth it.
basic.oneStory: This passage carries the Bible's story to its end. The death that entered through Adam meets its match in the risen Christ, the firstfruits of a new humanity. His resurrection guarantees ours, and His reign will not end until the last enemy, death, is destroyed and God is all in all. What began in a garden with a curse ends with a King who has emptied the grave.

context.literary:
Verses 12 to 34 are one carefully built argument, and its engine is the repeated word 'if.' Verses 12 to 19 run a chain of conditionals, each one a step down. If there is no resurrection of the dead, Christ is not raised, verse 13. If Christ is not raised, preaching and faith are worthless, verse 14. Then the apostles are false witnesses, verse 15, the Corinthians are still in their sins, verse 17, the dead in Christ have perished, verse 18, and the living are the most pitiable of all people, verse 19. Verse 16 repeats verse 13 almost word for word, as though Paul wanted to tap the same nail twice.

Then comes the hinge, one of the shortest and greatest sentences in the letter: 'But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead,' verse 20. Everything after it climbs back up. Verses 20 to 28 are a compressed account of history in three beats: Adam and Christ, verses 21 and 22; the order of the rising, 'each in his own turn,' verse 23; and the end, when the Son hands over the kingdom, verses 24 to 28. Scripture is woven into the sentences, Psalm 110:1 in verse 25 and Psalm 8:6 in verse 27.

The last section, verses 29 to 34, returns to the 'if' form and answers with practical arguments: the strange practice of being baptised for the dead, the daily danger Paul and his companions face, and a quotation from Isaiah and a line of Greek wisdom that conclude with a stern call to wake up. The passage thus moves from the logic of faith, to the grand sweep of history, to the ethics of the hour, and it ends not with a lecture but with a rebuke aimed at a church that had drifted.
context.historical:
The denial Paul faces probably came from the Greek cultural air that the Corinthians breathed. Most educated Greeks believed in some kind of life of the soul after death, but thought the body a prison or a burden to escape, and a raised body was a contradiction in terms. The Corinthians may have believed they were already spiritually risen and had nothing left to hope for, as Paul half suggests in 4:8 where he says with irony that they already had all they wanted and had already become rich, and as a later error in Ephesus claimed 'the resurrection has already occurred,' 2 Timothy 2:18. That makes the denial less a rejection of heaven than a rejection of a future bodily rising.

The picture of Adam would have been familiar to any who had heard the Genesis story, which Paul clearly taught them. The festival of firstfruits was an agricultural reality: in Israel, the first sheaf of the barley harvest was waved before the LORD on the day after the Sabbath, Leviticus 23:10 to 11, a promise that more was coming.

The reference to people 'baptized for the dead' in verse 29 is a real puzzle for historians, because we know of no clear parallel in the church at that time. Paul speaks of it as something 'they' do, not 'we.' Verse 32 mentions that he 'fought wild beasts in Ephesus.' That may be a figure for fierce opposition, as in the ancient world 'fighting beasts' could be a figure of speech, or it could be literal peril, and Paul's own list of sufferings in 2 Corinthians 11:23 to 27 shows he knew real danger. The quotation 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' is from Isaiah 22:13, said by people who refused to repent as judgment drew near, and 'Bad company corrupts good character' was a proverb of the Greek world, often traced to the poet Menander.
context.canonical:
The argument reads Genesis back through the cross. Verses 21 and 22 take the sentence of Genesis 3:19, 'to dust you shall return,' and set against it a second man. Paul unfolds the same pattern in Romans 5:12 to 19, where 'one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men.' Death came into the world through a man, and Paul insists that the answer must come through a man too.

Verse 20's firstfruits comes from Leviticus 23:9 to 14. The first sheaf was not itself the whole harvest; it was the part that guaranteed the rest. Colossians 1:18 gives Christ the matching title, 'the beginning and firstborn from among the dead.' Revelation 1:5 says the same.

Verses 25 to 27 weave two psalms together. Psalm 110:1, 'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet,' is among the most quoted Old Testament verses in the New Testament, and Peter and the writer to the Hebrews both apply it to the risen Christ, Acts 2:34 to 36 and Hebrews 1:13. Psalm 8:6, 'You have placed everything under his feet,' describes humanity's dominion, and Hebrews 2:8 to 9 says that we do not yet see everything subject to man, 'But we see Jesus.' Ephesians 1:20 to 22 applies the same words to Christ's exaltation.

The picture of last things sits with other texts: 1 Thessalonians 4:14 to 17 gives the order of the coming, John 5:28 to 29 the rising of all, and Revelation 20:14 the casting of Death and Hades into the lake of fire. The quotation in verse 32 is from Isaiah 22:13, where people faced with judgment chose revelry over repentance.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the Corinthians to see where their denial actually leads. He does not threaten them. He follows their own claim, step by step, to its bottom: if there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ is not raised, and if Christ is not raised, everything they have built on is air. A person can feel that one doctrine is optional until he sees what is hung on it.

He wanted them next to feel the other side. The turning sentence, 'But Christ has indeed been raised,' is meant to bring breath back into the room. Verses 20 to 28 are not a speculation about the end but a reassurance, saying that the story is under control, that death is a beaten foe waiting its turn to be destroyed, and that God will in the end be 'all in all.'

And he wanted holy living. The final paragraph says that belief in the resurrection has consequences: why risk your life, why resist temptation, why avoid bad company, if death ends everything? Paul's final line, 'Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning,' shows that he is after a changed way of life, not an academic victory. He closes with shame on purpose: some of them had a poor knowledge of God, and he said so 'to your shame,' verse 34, because he loved them enough to say it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter mostly describes what is true and what will be, and from it a few commands arise. The sequence of Adam and Christ, firstfruits and harvest, and the reign until death is destroyed is description of God's plan; it tells us what has happened and what is promised, and is not a set of instructions.

The commands are at the end: 'Do not be deceived,' 'Sober up as you ought, and stop sinning,' verses 33 and 34. These bind every reader. Hope in the resurrection is meant to make a person clear-headed and holy, and bad company is named as a real danger to character.

Two details need care. Verse 29, about people baptised for the dead, is something Paul mentions as a fact about others, in the third person, and he never commands or commends it. Reading it as an instruction invents a practice the text does not teach. And verse 32, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,' is a quotation of what people say when they have no hope, not Paul's advice. Describing a bad argument is not endorsing it. The verse's function is to show the conclusion that follows if the resurrection is false, and then to bring the reader back from it.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by those who are baptized for the dead in verse 29?

views.label: An argument from a practice Paul does not endorse
views.case: Paul refers to something some were doing, whatever it was, to expose its inconsistency: it makes no sense to be baptized for the dead if the dead are never raised. He argues from their own practice without commending it, and notably switches to they and them rather than we.

views.label: One of several proposed meanings
views.case: Others read it as baptism undertaken in hope of reunion with dead believers, or as normal baptism understood in relation to the dead. The wording is genuinely obscure, and the church has never agreed on the precise reference.

debates.bearing: On any reading, the verse does not establish a doctrine of vicarious baptism that saves the dead. Paul is not teaching salvation by proxy but pressing home that resurrection hope alone makes such actions coherent; the rest of Scripture ties salvation to personal faith in Christ, not to being baptized on someone else's behalf.

debates.question: How can the Son be subjected to the Father in verse 28 without being lesser than the Father?

views.label: The Son's saving mission, not His nature
views.case: The subjection describes the Son's role in accomplishing redemption as the incarnate mediator, handing the completed kingdom to the Father; it speaks of order and mission within the Godhead, not of any inequality of being.

views.label: A picture of the goal of redemption
views.case: The verse paints the final state in which God is all in all, the whole redeemed order gladly under God's unclouded reign through the Son, rather than making a metaphysical claim that the Son is inferior.

debates.bearing: The orthodox faith confesses the Son as fully and eternally God, equal with the Father; verse 28 describes the consummation of His saving work, not a lowering of His deity.

debates.question: Does 'in Christ all will be made alive' in verse 22 mean that everyone will finally be saved?

views.label: All people, without exception
views.case: Some read the two 'alls' of verse 22 as the same group, so that everyone who dies in Adam is made alive in Christ, and read 'God may be all in all,' verse 28, as the restoration of every creature.

views.label: All who are in Christ
views.case: Most readers hold that the second 'all' is limited by the words 'in Christ,' and by verse 23, 'those who belong to Him.' The same sentence speaks of enemies who are 'destroyed,' verses 24 to 26, and Paul warns of people who are ignorant of God, verse 34. Resurrection to life is for those united to Christ, while other texts speak of a resurrection to judgment, John 5:29.

debates.bearing: The passage's purpose is to ground the Christian hope of resurrection in Christ's own rising, not to answer the question of final destiny. Read with its immediate qualifiers and the wider testimony of Scripture, the church has understood it as the promise of life to those who belong to Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul says that without the resurrection the preaching is 'worthless' and the faith 'futile.' The Greek words differ. In verse 14 the word is kenos, 'empty, hollow,' like a vessel with nothing in it, and in verse 17 the word is mataios, 'futile, aimless,' faith that leads nowhere. One word says the message has no content, and the other says the believing has no result. Paul uses kenos again at the very end of the chapter, verse 58, to say that labour in the Lord is 'not in vain,' so the chapter begins in emptiness and ends in fullness.

The charge of being 'false witnesses' in verse 15 translates pseudomartyres. The word martys, 'witness,' is the root of the English 'martyr,' and the language is legal. The apostles had given testimony in God's court; if Christ is not raised, they have sworn to something God did not do. The stakes are therefore about God's own truthfulness and not only about hope.

In verses 22 and 45 the verb for 'made alive' is zoopoieo, to give life, to cause to live. It is used of God's life-giving work, as in John 5:21 and Romans 4:17, and the same word appears of Christ as 'a life-giving spirit' in verse 45. In verse 22 the passive voice says that life is given, and it is not something a person achieves.

Verse 23 says 'each in his own turn,' en to idio tagmati. The noun tagma was a military term for a rank or division, an ordered company. Paul sees the resurrection as an orderly advance in ranks: Christ first, then those who belong to Him, then the end. The word telos in verse 24, 'the end,' means a goal reached and not just a stopping point.

Twice Paul says that enemies will be 'destroyed,' verses 24 and 26, from katargeo. The verb means to render inoperative, to strip of power, and does not necessarily mean to annihilate. It is the same verb used of death's defeat in 2 Timothy 1:10. The enemy is disarmed and put out of work. Paul also uses hypotasso, 'to put in subjection,' repeatedly in verses 27 and 28, which gives the passage its sense of an ordered handing over of authority. The Son is subjected to the Father, and all things are subjected to the Son.

In verse 29, the phrase is huper ton nekron, 'for the dead,' where huper is a flexible preposition: 'on behalf of,' 'for the sake of,' or 'with a view to.' The flexibility is one reason the verse has so many readings.

Two details of the closing verses are worth noting. In verse 32 Paul says he 'fought wild beasts,' from the verb etheriomachesa, which may be literal or figurative. And in verse 34 'sober up' is eknepsate, a word for coming out of drunkenness, a call to wake up, and the 'ignorance of God' there is agnosia, which names a positive lack of knowledge and not an innocent not-knowing.

typology.fulfillment: In Leviticus 23:10 to 11 the Israelites were to bring a sheaf of the firstfruits to the priest, who waved it before the LORD 'on the day after the Sabbath' so that it might be accepted on their behalf. The sheaf was a pledge that the harvest was God's and was coming. Christ was raised on the first day of the week, and Paul says He is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The escalation is that the sheaf stood for a crop of grain, while Christ stands for a harvest of people. The type falls short in that the Levitical sheaf was only a sign of what would come, whereas the risen Christ is Himself the guarantee and the first instalment of the same kind of life.

typology.type: The first man and the last
typology.fulfillment: Adam was the head of a race, and what he did bound those in him, Genesis 3:17 to 19. Paul says that 'as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive,' verse 22, and in Romans 5:14 he calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come.' The correspondence is headship: one man acting for many. The escalation is that Christ's gift is greater than Adam's loss, as Romans 5:17 says, 'how much more.' The type falls short because Adam's act brought death by his disobedience, whereas Christ's obedience brings life by grace, and the two are not simply mirror images.

Psalm 8:6 celebrates humanity crowned with glory and given rule over the works of God's hands, 'everything under his feet.' Genesis 1:26 to 28 gave that dominion at creation, and sin left it unfulfilled. Hebrews 2:8 to 9 says, 'at present we do not see everything subject to him. But we see Jesus.' Paul sees Jesus as the Man who has taken up the dominion lost by the first Adam and who will bring everything, death included, under His feet. The type is not yet complete, since the last enemy still awaits its end.

After Israel's victory at Gibeon, Joshua told his commanders to 'put your feet on the necks of these kings,' Joshua 10:24, as a sign that every enemy would be defeated, and the Lord had promised His Anointed, 'until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet,' Psalm 110:1. The picture is of a king who has not just beaten rivals but subdued them in the open. In Christ it deepens, because the enemies are not nations but dominion, authority, power and death, verses 24 to 26. The type falls short in that Joshua's victory could be won in a day, while Christ's reign unfolds in stages until the last enemy falls.

study.christ:
The whole argument is built on one fact about Christ, that He has been raised, and then unfolds what follows. First, Christ is the firstfruits. The word 'first' implies others after Him. His resurrection is not a private miracle but the beginning of a harvest, and those who belong to Him will follow, verse 23. Colossians 1:18 calls Him 'the beginning and firstborn from among the dead,' and Romans 8:29 says He is 'the firstborn among many brothers.' To believe in Christ's rising is to believe in the rising of His people.

Second, Christ is the second Adam. Death came through a man, so the answer comes through a man, verse 21. Paul's concern is that the answer must be fully human. A Saviour who only seemed to be a man could not undo the loss that came through a man. Hebrews 2:14 says that He shared in flesh and blood 'so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death.' The resurrection is the reversal of Adam's sentence, and it is accomplished by one who stood in Adam's place.

Third, Christ is the reigning King. He sits at God's right hand, Psalm 110:1, and His reign has a purpose: He must reign 'until He has put all His enemies under His feet,' verse 25. Ephesians 1:20 to 22 says that this has begun, since God raised Him, seated Him at His right hand far above all rule and authority, and 'put everything under His feet.' The present age is the time between a decisive victory and its full application, and Christians live in that interval.

Fourth, Christ is the one who will finish the work. The last enemy, death, will be destroyed by Him, verse 26, and then He 'hands over the kingdom to God the Father.' It is not that He steps down but that He presents what He has won. The Son who came to do the Father's will, John 6:38, completes it, and in doing so remains what He has always been, God the Son.

Fifth, Christ is the life of His people. Jesus said to Martha, 'I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies,' John 11:25. In verse 22 the phrase 'in Christ' says where life is found. We are not made alive by an idea about Him but by being joined to Him.

A word of care is needed. The subjection of the Son in verse 28 is not a sign that He is less than God; the church has long read it as the completion of His mission as mediator. And the firstfruits picture, while rich, should not be pressed further than Paul presses it. He uses it for the order and the guarantee of the resurrection, not as a calendar proof text about the day of the week.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who is faithful to His own word. The deepest worry of verse 15 is that if Christ is not raised, then the apostles have testified falsely 'about God.' Paul regards the resurrection as God's own signature on the gospel, so that to deny it is to charge God with a lie. The God of the Bible is truthful, and the whole Christian hope rests on that.

He is the God who raises. The language is passive throughout, 'Christ has been raised,' and 'will be made alive,' and behind the passive is the active hand of God. Jesus rebuked the Sadducees that they knew neither the Scriptures nor the power of God, Matthew 22:29, and Paul's argument is a longer version of the same rebuke. The God who made life from dust in Genesis 2:7 is not stuck when the body returns to dust.

He is sovereign over history. In verses 24 to 28 there is a plan with stages: the rising of Christ, the rising of His people at His coming, then the end. Nothing is out of control. The enemies, whatever their names, are dominion, authority and power, and they will be rendered powerless in due order. Death in particular is not an equal rival to God but a last enemy waiting to be destroyed.

He is a God of order. The word 'each in his own turn' reminds us of the ranks of an army and the order of the Spirit's work in the church in chapter 14. His timetable is not hurried or random.

He is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Verse 28 is one of the clearest windows into the relations of the persons. The Son hands over the kingdom to the Father, not as a lesser being but as the one who completes a mission, and the goal is 'that God may be all in all.' The passage presumes the Father's authority, the Son's mediating work, and elsewhere in the chapter the Spirit who gives life. The doctrine of the Trinity is not argued here; it is assumed, and everything in the plan of salvation depends on it.

He is just and merciful. The same God who gives life to those in Christ says that enemies will be destroyed and that some are ignorant of Him. The passage does not soften that. Yet its note is hope, because the one who has the power to judge has also done the work of rescue.

For worship, the passage invites steadiness. In verse 19 Paul says that hope in Christ for this life alone would be pitiful, and in verse 34 he tells us to wake up. The right response to a God who raises the dead is clear-headed gratitude, a changed life, and a willingness to take risks for His sake, since the end of the story is already known.

crossReferences.note: Paul's fullest comparison of Adam and Christ. Sin and death came through one man, and grace and life come through another, with the gift far outweighing the fall. It is the long form of verses 21 and 22 and explains why the answer to death has to come through a man.

'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' Verse 25 gives this psalm as the reason Christ must reign until all enemies are subdued. It places the risen Lord on a throne with a promise attached: victory is guaranteed, but its completion lies ahead.

The verse about humanity ruling 'the works of Your hands' with everything under his feet. Paul uses it in verse 27 for Christ, who recovers the dominion Adam lost. Hebrews 2:6 to 9 makes the same move, so the psalm about man becomes a psalm about the Man.

'Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire.' This is the vision of verse 26 in picture form, when the last enemy is finally destroyed. It shows that the defeat of death is not a metaphor for comfort but a real event that closes the age.

Paul comforts the grieving with the same logic: since Jesus died and rose, God will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep in Him. It complements verse 23, 'then at His coming, those who belong to Him,' by describing what happens when He comes.

The law of the first sheaf, waved before the LORD on the day after the Sabbath so that it would be accepted for the people. It is the background to 'firstfruits' in verse 20, and it shows why one sheaf could stand for a whole field.

The sentence on Adam, ending with 'to dust you shall return.' Verse 21 answers it: since death came through a man, resurrection comes through a man. The curse that closed the first garden is the problem the chapter sets out to solve.

Christ is called 'the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence.' It repeats the firstfruits claim in another figure, and adds that His place as first is a place of supremacy over everything.

God raised Christ, seated Him at His right hand far above every power, and 'put everything under His feet.' It shows that the quotation of Psalm 8 in verse 27 was a standard way of speaking about the exalted Christ, and that the subjection has already begun.

The source of 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.' In Isaiah it was said by people who ignored the Lord's call to repent and chose revelry in the face of judgment. Paul sets the same words at the end of a world without resurrection, to show where unbelief goes.

'I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies.' Jesus says of Himself what Paul argues here: resurrection is not only a future event but a person, and life is found in being joined to Him.

study.oneStory:
The chapter answers the sentence of Genesis 3:19, 'to dust you shall return,' with a promise. From the moment of the fall, the question hung over the story: would the death that entered with Adam have the last word? Eden's closed gate and flaming sword guarded the way to the tree of life, and the generations of Genesis 5 end again and again with 'and then he died.' The patriarchs were buried in a field they had bought, as if death was an owner.

The Old Testament pressed hope through that darkness. Job spoke of seeing his Redeemer in his flesh, Job 19:25 to 27. Isaiah 25:8 said that God would swallow up death for ever, and Daniel 12:2 said that many who sleep in the dust of the earth would awake. Those texts were not yet joined into a plan, and they left their readers with promises and no firstfruits.

Verse 20 is the point at which the promise becomes an event. Christ is raised, and Paul reads that raising as the first act of a larger harvest. The passage lays out the story in stages: the first man, Adam, who brought death; the last Adam, Christ, who brings life; the reign of Christ now, with enemies still under His feet in process; His coming, when those who belong to Him are raised; and the end, when He hands the kingdom to the Father.

In the rest of the New Testament, this is the shape of Christian waiting. Believers are people who live between the firstfruits and the harvest, who have the Spirit as a down payment, 2 Corinthians 1:22, and who groan with the creation while they wait for the redemption of the body, Romans 8:23. The practical turn at the end of the passage, to stop sinning and shun bad company, comes from the same place. A person who knows how the story ends can live now in the light of it.

The Bible's last chapters complete the sentence. The enemy that Paul says will be destroyed last is destroyed, Revelation 20:14, and the curse of Genesis 3 is lifted, 'No longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3. The tree of life is open to the people of God, and the Lord God Himself is with them. When Paul says that God will be 'all in all,' he means exactly this: the creation that began with God's good word ends with God's undivided presence, and death has no place in it.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say the resurrection of the dead cannot be denied?

options.text: Because if the dead are not raised, then not even Christ has been raised, and the gospel collapses.
options.note: The two rise and fall together; deny one and you lose the other.

options.text: Because the resurrection is promised throughout the Old Testament.
options.note: There is Old Testament hope of resurrection, but Paul's point here is that denying it denies Christ's own resurrection.

options.text: Because Greek philosophy required it.
options.note: Greek thought tended to deny bodily resurrection; Paul argues against that.

options.text: Because the dead have already been seen rising.
options.note: Paul grounds it in Christ's resurrection, not in observed risings of others.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Christ is the firstfruits?

options.text: His resurrection is the first installment and sure pledge of the resurrection of all who belong to Him.
options.note: Where the firstfruits are raised, the harvest must follow.

options.text: He was simply the first person ever to come back to life.
options.note: Others were revived before, but firstfruits means His rising guarantees ours.

options.text: He is the best example of a good life.
options.note: Firstfruits is about resurrection and harvest, not merely example.

options.text: His resurrection has nothing to do with ours.
options.note: The whole point is that His rising secures ours.

quiz.q: How does Paul contrast Adam and Christ?

options.text: As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.
options.note: Two heads of humanity: death through one, life through the other.

options.text: Adam brought sin and Christ brought forgiveness, but not new life.
options.note: Partly right, yet Paul's stress falls on death through Adam and resurrection life through Christ.

options.text: Adam brought life and Christ brought death.
options.note: It is the reverse: death through Adam, life through Christ.

options.text: Both simply teach us to live well.
options.note: The contrast is about death and resurrection life, not mere teaching.

quiz.q: What is the last enemy to be destroyed?

options.text: Death.
options.note: The last enemy to be destroyed is death, verse 26.

options.text: Human governments.
options.note: Christ subdues all rule and authority, but the last enemy named is death.

options.text: Satan alone.
options.note: Hostile powers are subdued, but Paul names death as the final enemy.

options.text: Nothing; the world simply continues as it is.
options.note: Paul promises the destruction of death, not the status quo.

quiz.q: How should the resurrection shape the way believers live?

options.text: It grounds courage, sacrifice, and holy living, so we sober up and stop sinning.
options.note: If the dead are raised, risk and holiness make sense; verses 32 to 34.

options.text: It means we can live for pleasure since nothing matters.
options.note: That is the very attitude Paul rejects, let us eat and drink.

options.text: It means we should withdraw from all danger.
options.note: Paul embraces daily danger precisely because of the resurrection.

options.text: It mainly comforts us about the future but changes little now.
options.note: It does give future comfort, yet Paul draws present consequences: courage, sacrifice, and holiness.

quiz.q: How should we understand baptism for the dead in verse 29?

options.text: Paul argues from a practice without endorsing it, and the verse does not teach salvation by proxy.
options.note: He presses its inconsistency if the dead are not raised; Scripture ties salvation to personal faith.

options.text: It establishes that we can be saved through someone else's baptism.
options.note: The passage does not teach vicarious baptism for salvation.

options.text: The meaning is genuinely obscure and disputed.
options.note: True, the reference is unclear, but Paul's point is that resurrection alone makes such acts coherent.

options.text: It shows the early church practiced baptism for the dead as a model for us.
options.note: Paul mentions a practice but does not commend it as a model to follow.

questions: Paul says that without the resurrection, faith is futile and we are still in our sins. How does the certainty of Christ's resurrection change the weight of your daily struggles?
Christ is the firstfruits, the guarantee of the harvest. How does knowing your own resurrection is secured in His shape the way you face loss and death?
The risen Christ reigns until every enemy is under His feet. Where do you need to trust that the powers troubling you are already being subdued?
If there were no resurrection, Paul says we may as well eat and drink for tomorrow we die. How does resurrection hope free you to sacrifice and take risks for Christ?
Paul ends by calling the church to sober up and stop sinning. What would it look like for resurrection hope to make you more, not less, serious about holiness?

translationNotes.note: Firstfruits translates aparche, the first portion of harvest offered to God as a pledge of the full crop; the image guarantees the resurrection of all who belong to Christ.

Baptized for the dead is one of the most debated phrases in the letter. Paul reasons from a practice without endorsing it, and switches to they and them; the verse does not establish a doctrine of saving baptism performed on behalf of the dead.
Fought wild beasts in Ephesus is likely a vivid figure for fierce human opposition rather than a literal arena; the quoted line, let us eat and drink, echoes Isaiah 22:13.
